analysis.one_liner: Bans new oil and gas drilling beneath the Great Lakes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: it was referred to a Resources Committee subcommittee in March 1999 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for anyone to drill for oil or gas under any of the Great Lakes, including slant or directional drilling from shore that angles under the lakebed. The Attorney General could sue in federal court to enforce the ban. The bill was introduced by Rep. Bart Stupak of Michigan and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee. No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million people whose drinking water comes from the Great Lakes, plus the region's tourism and fishing economies, gain protection from the risk of spills, leaks, and contaminated water that offshore drilling brings. Existing shore-adjacent landowners also avoid industrial drilling activity on nearby lakeshores.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Great Lakes region residents and water users

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits all drilling activity to extract oil or gas from submerged lands under the Great Lakes, expressly including slant and directional drilling, so operators could not drill from shore and angle under the lakebed [S2] [S3].
It gives the Attorney General of the United States the power to bring a federal lawsuit to enforce the ban, rather than leaving enforcement to case-by-case state action [S2] [S3].
The prohibition applies to all of the Great Lakes as defined by the Great Lakes Fishery Act of 1956, closing a regional loophole before any new drilling could begin [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that might have drilled under the lakes lose access to those reserves, and states bordering the lakes forgo potential lease revenue and royalties from drilling beneath the lakebed.

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently lock away oil and gas reserves under the lakes, and the bordering states would forgo lease royalties and any local economic activity the drilling might have generated [S2].

The federal ban overrides state land and mineral decisions; a state such as Michigan might have preferred to allow carefully regulated directional drilling and collect its own revenue rather than have Congress decide for it [S3].
Enforcement runs through federal court actions by the Attorney General, which can be slow and depend on the priorities of whichever administration holds office [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is permanent protection of the world's largest freshwater system — the drinking water source for tens of millions of people — from the spill and leak risks of drilling under or beside the lakes. The cost is modest by comparison: forgone royalties and reserves of unknown size, in a region whose economy depends heavily on clean water and tourism. On balance the trade strongly favors protection, though a state that wanted the revenue had a fair complaint about Congress deciding the question.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Resources Committee, which passed it along to an energy subcommittee, and it sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak of Michigan introduced the bill on March 18, 1999 with 13 original cosponsors including members from Ohio, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Massachusetts [S1] [S3].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources [S5].
Six days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it remained for the rest of the Congress [S5].
By the end of the session the bill had 18 cosponsors, 16 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but the committee never acted and the House never voted [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests benefited from the bill's death, since no federal ban now stood in the way of drilling beneath the Great Lakes; the lakes themselves got no added federal protection from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 16 of 18 cosponsors were Democrats, with 2 Republicans joining; no Republican committee action moved the bill, and its fate rested with a committee that never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have closed all of the Great Lakes' submerged lands to oil and gas extraction, including directional drilling from shore under the lakebed. The industry's interest in keeping those reserves open runs against the region's drinking water and shoreline economy, which bear the spill and leak risk.

Clean water underpins the region's recreation, tourism, and commercial fishing. Banning drilling beneath the lakes protects the resource these industries depend on, and their interests run alongside those of residents who drink the water.
